llm_response.content:
Below is a complete plan for estimating the causal capitalization of assigned public school characteristics into single-family home prices in Mecklenburg County, leveraging sharp reassignments from court-driven boundary changes and the fine spatial detail in the parcel data.

1. Identification Strategy
I will use a boundary-discontinuity difference-in-differences/event-study design that exploits:
- Space: sharp discontinuities in school assignment at attendance boundaries among homes in very close proximity, so local neighborhood amenities are comparable.
- Time: large, administratively driven reassignment events in 1997 (high school) and 1998 (elementary and middle) that change a parcel’s assigned school(s) while the house and neighborhood remain the same.

Two complementary estimators:
A. Boundary-DD hedonic (main): Cross-sectional within-year comparisons of homes on opposite sides of the same boundary segment-year, with ultra-flexible boundary-segment-by-year fixed effects. Identification arises from the fact that within a micro-boundary segment-year, two otherwise similar homes face different assigned schools.
B. Event study among reassigned parcels (validation): For parcels that are reassigned, estimate dynamic price paths before and after the reassignment using parcel fixed effects. This tests pre-trends and anticipatory effects.

To separate “schools themselves” from correlated neighborhood composition and sorting:
- We (i) restrict to very close-to-boundary homes so amenities are locally comparable, (ii) absorb local time-varying shocks with boundary-segment-by-year FE, and (iii) use reassignment-induced, plausibly exogenous changes in school characteristics. We also leverage school value-added (constructed from student microdata) to approximate school effectiveness apart from peer composition and include separate controls for peer composition (race/FRL shares) and average scores.

2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable:
  - Continuous: the assigned school characteristics to which the parcel is zoned in the sale year, measured as lagged school-year attributes to avoid simultaneity (e.g., value-added z-score, mean test score z-score, Black share, FRL share), separately for elementary, middle, and high school.
  - For event-study plots: indicator that a parcel’s assigned school (at a given level) changes in the reassignment year.

- Control group:
  - Boundary-DD: Homes located on the other side of the same micro-boundary segment-year (within a narrow buffer), which face a different assigned school but share the same local boundary-year fixed effect.
  - Event study: The same parcels in pre-periods (parcel fixed effects), with homes that are not reassigned serving as an auxiliary check (not the main counterfactual).

- Treatment timing / event date:
  - High school reassignment: school year starting Fall 1997.
  - Elementary/middle reassignment: school year starting Fall 1998.
  - We will treat the event date as the school-board adoption date if available; if not, we will use the first school year of implementation, and test for pre-trends to detect anticipation.

- Running variable and cutoff:
  - Not an RDD as the main design, but we will implement boundary buffers (e.g., within 0.5–1.0 km of a boundary) to ensure local comparability.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- A1. Local comparability at boundaries (cross-sectional): Within a very small distance of an attendance boundary, housing and neighborhood amenities vary smoothly; discontinuities in prices reflect differences in assigned schools. Plausibility: The district’s use of busing, satellites, and non-contiguous zones deliberately breaks correlation between neighborhood traits and school assignment; sharp differences in assignment exist for nearby parcels.

- A2. As-good-as-random reassignment within micro-boundaries (over time): Boundary redraws are driven by legal desegregation constraints, capacity, and new school openings, not by micro-boundary house price trends. Plausibility: Reassignments affected large shares of parcels (30% in 1997 HS; ~16–18% 1998 E/M) linked to legal mandates and growth, making targeted manipulation of micro-boundary segments unlikely.

- A3. No differential local shocks coincident with reassignment across sides of the same boundary-segment-year: Any local time-varying amenities (e.g., roadwork) are absorbed by boundary-segment-by-year FE. Plausibility: The FE absorb virtually all local, time-varying factors common to both sides of the micro-segment.

- A4. Limited anticipation and sorting on unobservables at the exact time-location of treatment: Householders did not perfectly time sales or remodels exactly around boundary changes in a way correlated with unobservables. Plausibility: We can test for pre-trends in the event-study and for stable listing/sales composition around the event; the administrative timing and wide scope reduce scope for precise manipulation.

- A5. School quality measures capture the “school” component rather than only peers: Using school value-added (constructed from gains) and including separate controls for mean scores and composition helps isolate school effectiveness from peer composition. Plausibility: VA is closer to school effectiveness than levels; including both VA and composition allows decomposition of capitalization.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigations
- T1. Anticipation and endogenous sale timing: Owners could accelerate/delay sales in response to announced redistricting.
  - Mitigation: Use event-study leads to test for pre-trends; redefine event to the announcement date if available; exclude sales in narrow windows around announcement; use last-ask-to-sale intervals if available to detect timing shifts; re-estimate on repeat-sales only.

- T2. New school construction externalities unrelated to assignment (e.g., noise, traffic, new amenities from proximity to a new building):
  - Mitigation: Control flexibly for distance to nearest school and to newly opened schools interacted with post; compare parcels equidistant on both sides within the same micro-boundary segment; add boundary-segment-by-year FE, which nets out any local year-specific shocks; run robustness excluding parcels within small radii (e.g., <0.5 km) of newly built schools.

- T3. Measurement error and simultaneity in school attributes:
  - Mitigation: Use lagged school attributes (t-1) to predict prices at time t; where possible, instrument assigned school “quality” with reassignment exposure interacted with pre-period old-vs-new school attribute differences (a leave-one-out/predicted delta) to address measurement error and remaining simultaneity.

5. R Code Outline
Notes:
- Assume CSVs exist that provide: parcel-level sales, structural attributes, tax-assessor neighborhood, boundary segment IDs and distances, annual school assignments by level, school characteristics by level-year, and the year each parcel is first reassigned at each level.
- We focus on a boundary-buffer sample (e.g., within 1 km of a boundary).
- We run (i) the boundary-DD hedonic with boundary-segment-by-year FE and (ii) an event-study among reassigned parcels with parcel FE.
- We show one IV robustness that instruments assigned school quality with predicted delta quality implied by reassignment and pre-period school attributes.

R code:

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(lubridate)

# 1) Load data
sales <- fread("sales.csv")  # parcel_id, sale_date, price, beds, baths, sqft, age, quality, lat, lon, nbhd_id
assign <- fread("assignments.csv")  # parcel_id, year, elem_id, mid_id, high_id
schools <- fread("schools.csv")  # school_id, year, mean_score_z, value_added_z, black_share, frl_share
bound <- fread("boundary_parcels.csv")  # parcel_id, segment_id, dist_to_boundary_km
reassign <- fread("reassignment_events.csv")  # parcel_id, level (E/M/H), event_year_level

# 2) Prep variables
# Sales timing
sales[, sale_date := ymd(sale_date)]
sales[, sale_year := year(sale_date)]
sales[, sale_month := floor_date(sale_date, "month")]
sales[, lprice := log(price)]

# Merge assignments (use school attributes lagged by 1 year)
# First, merge sale-year assignment
setkey(assign, parcel_id, year)
setkey(sales, parcel_id, sale_year)
dat <- merge(sales, assign, by.x = c("parcel_id","sale_year"), by.y = c("parcel_id","year"), all.x = TRUE)

# Merge school characteristics by level, lagged one year relative to sale year
lag_year <- function(y) y - 1L
# Elementary
setnames(schools, old=c("school_id","year","mean_score_z","value_added_z","black_share","frl_share"),
                 new=c("school_id_e","year_e","mean_z_e","va_z_e","black_e","frl_e"))
setkey(schools, school_id_e, year_e)
dat[, year_e := lag_year(sale_year)]
dat <- merge(dat, schools, by.x = c("elem_id","year_e"), by.y = c("school_id_e","year_e"), all.x = TRUE)

# Middle
schools_m <- fread("schools.csv")
setnames(schools_m, old=c("school_id","year","mean_score_z","value_added_z","black_share","frl_share"),
                    new=c("school_id_m","year_m","mean_z_m","va_z_m","black_m","frl_m"))
setkey(schools_m, school_id_m, year_m)
dat[, year_m := lag_year(sale_year)]
dat <- merge(dat, schools_m, by.x = c("mid_id","year_m"), by.y = c("school_id_m","year_m"), all.x = TRUE)

# High
schools_h <- fread("schools.csv")
setnames(schools_h, old=c("school_id","year","mean_score_z","value_added_z","black_share","frl_share"),
                    new=c("school_id_h","year_h","mean_z_h","va_z_h","black_h","frl_h"))
setkey(schools_h, school_id_h, year_h)
dat[, year_h := lag_year(sale_year)]
dat <- merge(dat, schools_h, by.x = c("high_id","year_h"), by.y = c("school_id_h","year_h"), all.x = TRUE)

# Merge boundary info
dat <- merge(dat, bound, by = "parcel_id", all.x = TRUE)

# Boundary buffer: within 1 km of any boundary
dat_buf <- dat[dist_to_boundary_km <= 1]

# 3) Main boundary-DD hedonic
# Flexible local controls via boundary-segment-by-year FE; include structural controls
# Cluster at boundary-segment level
fml_main <- lprice ~ va_z_e + va_z_m + va_z_h + mean_z_e + mean_z_m + mean_z_h +
                     black_e + black_m + black_h + frl_e + frl_m + frl_h +
                     beds + baths + sqft + age + I(age^2) + quality
fe_main <- ~ i(segment_id, sale_year)  # boundary-segment-by-year FE

est_main <- feols(fml_main, fe = fe_main, cluster = ~ segment_id, data = dat_buf)
summary(est_main)

# 4) Event-study among reassigned parcels (parcel FE)
# Build event time for each level; example shown for high school 1997 wave
# Merge reassignment events
dat_ev <- merge(dat, reassign[level == "H"], by = "parcel_id", all.x = TRUE, suffixes = c("", "_H"))
dat_ev[, event_time_H := sale_year - event_year_level]  # NA if never reassigned
# Keep parcels with a defined event and sales in a symmetric window
window <- 4L
es_sample <- dat_ev[!is.na(event_time_H) & event_time_H %between% c(-window, +window)]

# Sun & Abraham type event-study
es_est <- feols(lprice ~ sunab(event_year_level, sale_year) +
                          beds + baths + sqft + age + I(age^2) + quality |
                          parcel_id,  # parcel FE
                cluster = ~ high_id, data = es_sample)
summary(es_est)
iplot(es_est)  # visualize dynamic effects

# 5) IV robustness to address measurement error/simultaneity
# Construct instrument: for parcels reassigned at a level, instrument current assigned school VA with
# predicted delta = (pre-period avg VA of new school) - (pre-period avg VA of old school); zero for non-reassigned.
# Assume a CSV exists with pre-period averages by school_id: preavg_school.csv (school_id, va_preavg, mean_preavg, etc.)
preavg <- fread("preavg_school.csv")
setkey(preavg, school_id)
# Merge pre-averages for old and new schools; suppose reassignments.csv has old_id, new_id, level, event_year
reas <- fread("reassignments_detailed.csv")  # parcel_id, level, event_year, old_id, new_id
reas <- merge(reas, preavg, by.x = "old_id", by.y = "school_id", all.x = TRUE)
setnames(reas, "va_preavg", "va_old_pre")
reas <- merge(reas, preavg, by.x = "new_id", by.y = "school_id", all.x = TRUE)
setnames(reas, "va_preavg", "va_new_pre")
reas[, z_va_delta := va_new_pre - va_old_pre]
# Merge instrument back to sales data (example for high school)
dat_iv <- merge(dat_buf, reas[level == "H", .(parcel_id, event_year, z_va_delta)],
                by = "parcel_id", all.x = TRUE)
# Define instrument active only post-event for reassigned parcels; zero otherwise
dat_iv[, post_H := +(sale_year >= event_year)]
dat_iv[is.na(post_H), post_H := 0]
dat_iv[, z_va_H := fifelse(post_H == 1 & !is.na(z_va_delta), z_va_delta, 0)]

# 2SLS: instrument current assigned high-school VA with z_va_H; keep segment-year FE
iv_est <- feols(lprice ~ va_z_h + va_z_e + va_z_m + mean_z_e + mean_z_m + mean_z_h +
                         black_e + black_m + black_h + frl_e + frl_m + frl_h +
                         beds + baths + sqft + age + I(age^2) + quality |
                         i(segment_id, sale_year) | 
                         va_z_h ~ z_va_H,
                cluster = ~ segment_id, data = dat_iv)
summary(iv_est)

# 6) Robustness: narrower boundary buffer (<= 0.5 km) and exclude parcels near new school sites
dat_buf_narrow <- dat[dist_to_boundary_km <= 0.5]
est_narrow <- feols(fml_main, fe = fe_main, cluster = ~ segment_id, data = dat_buf_narrow)
summary(est_narrow)
```

Notes:
- If many parcels sell only once, the event-study relies on a subset with repeat transactions or at least pre/post representation; the boundary-DD hedonic uses all cross-sectional sales near boundaries.
- We cluster standard errors at boundary segment, but clustering at the school-year or school-pair level is an alternative robustness.

6. Expected Results
- Direction: Positive capitalization of school quality. A one standard deviation increase in school value-added should increase nearby home prices. Mean test scores will also capitalize but partly reflect peers; controlling for VA and composition should attenuate mean-score coefficients.
- Magnitude (priors):
  - School value-added: 1–3% higher price per 1 SD increase in VA at the most relevant level (likely strongest for elementary and middle for families with near-term attendance).
  - Peer composition: Higher FRL share and Black share likely correlate with lower prices even conditional on VA (revealed preferences, perceived future peers), on the order of 0.5–1.5% per 10 percentage point increase, though desegregation may compress these effects.
  - Mean test scores: Positive, but smaller once VA and composition included, perhaps 0–1% per 1 SD.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
- C1: Parallel trends/No differential pre-trends within micro-boundaries (event-study leads are flat) — 1
- C2: Exogenous treatment timing relative to micro-boundary housing markets (court-driven, capacity-driven redraws) — 1
- C3: Local continuity of non-school amenities at boundaries and use of boundary-segment-by-year FE — 1
- C4: Limited spillovers and confounding from new school construction externalities, addressed via distance controls/exclusions — 0.5
- C5: Correct inference and sufficient power (SEs clustered at boundary segment; multiple large reassignment events provide variation) — 1

Total: 4.5/5

This plan isolates capitalization of assigned schools by comparing very close neighbors across boundaries and exploiting plausibly exogenous reassignment shocks over time, while separating school effectiveness (value-added) from peer composition and test-score levels.
